title: Hydration Basics: How Much Water Do You Need?
content:
Water makes up about 60 percent of adult body weight and is essential for nearly every bodily function, including transporting nutrients, regulating temperature, and removing waste.

The National Academies of Sciences recommends a total daily water intake of about 3.7 litres (125 oz) for men and 2.7 litres (91 oz) for women, counting all beverages and the water content of food. About 20 percent of daily water intake typically comes from food.

Thirst is generally a reliable guide for healthy adults, but certain situations increase your fluid needs: hot or humid weather, physical activity, fever, vomiting, and diarrhoea all cause extra fluid loss. During vigorous exercise, the body can lose more than one litre of sweat per hour.

Signs of mild dehydration include dark yellow urine, dry mouth, headache, and fatigue. Severe dehydration — marked by rapid heartbeat, dizziness, and confusion — requires immediate medical attention.

Plain water is the best choice for hydration. Unsweetened tea and coffee also contribute to fluid intake. Sugar-sweetened beverages provide fluid but add calories and are associated with weight gain and dental problems when consumed regularly.

Older adults are at higher risk of dehydration because the sense of thirst diminishes with age. Kidney disease, heart failure, and certain medications (including diuretics) can alter fluid needs; if you have any of these conditions, ask your healthcare provider about your specific fluid targets.
source: Original — based on National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine 2005 DRI report (public domain summary) and CDC hydration guidance
